newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais rescue could top $23 billion.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais rescue could top $23 billion.

text.p: The final cost to the French government of saving state-controlled bank Credit Lyonnais could be far higher than a recent estimate of 130 billion francs ($23 billion), an official close to the rescue operation said on Wednesday.

The Consortium de Realisation (CDR), the state-backed agency selling off Credit Lyonnais assets as part of a recovery plan for the bank, told the parliamentary finance commission it expected the cost of its disposal operation to total 102 billion francs, a spokesman for the CDR said.
But that sum did not include carrying costs, expected to be around 30 billion francs, or the government's newest aid plan for the bank to ready it for sale in early 1999.
"It could go above 130 billion francs when you take into account the recapitalisation," the official close to the operation said.
The 130 billion franc estimate of the cost to the government of the rescue had come last week from a member of the finance commission, Patrick Devedjian.
Credit Lyonnais, which is expected to report a small profit for 1996 on Thursday, because of two state rescues, posted total losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994.
The red ink was the result of an ill-fated expansion binge at the end of the 1980s and the beginning of the 1990s.

Under the newest aid plan, promised for delivery to the European Commission for approval by the end of March, but which now could land in early April, the bank is expected to receive a 10 billion to 15 billion franc injection of public money.

That money will be needed to boost solvency ratios to attract a buyer and cover losses on asset sales sought by the European Commission in exchange for sanctioning the aid package, which will be the third in four years.

The Commission has estimated a further 15 billion to 20 billion francs in state money could be needed to soften the terms of loan the bank made under the 1995 rescue to finance the spinoff of assets from its balance sheet to the CDR.
Finance Ministry Jean Arthuis said in February the total cost of the rescue to the government could be at least 50 billion francs and has declined to comment on new estimates.

Michel Rouger, chairman of CDR, told the finance commission that out of the 102 billion in losses for his agency, some 85.6 billion francs were expected from sale of 190 billion francs of assets and loans that were transferred to it from the bank under the 1995 rescue.

A further 11.4 billion francs in losses were expected from off-balance sheet commitments while overhead charges for the CDR were expected to be five billion francs, the spokesman for the CDR said, relaying Rouger's comments to the commission.
The CDR was set up in 1995 to siphon off Credit Lyonnais's bad assets and clean up balance sheet.
The CDR said by mid-1997, it will have disposed of half of the activities transferred to it. It said that so far it had recuperated more than 70 percent of the book value of those assets and loans.

But the CDR spokesman warned the sale of the remaining Credit Lyonnais assets would be much harder. "The rest will be clearly more difficult," he said. "The easiest disposals were done first." But he said there had been "no fire sales."

He said Rouger had set a target of disposing of some 75 percent of the 190 billion francs in assets before 1999. Under the law, all of the assets must be disposed of by the year 2014. ($ = 5.65 French Francs)
